Fitzy already took you through the highlights (such as they were) from yesterday's press conference. We've gotten plenty used to the front office telling us about how pained they are by failing to meet their goals, so there wasn't much actual news in that sense. But we did get some actual substantive information regarding Roman Anthony. After a lost season that saw him bow out of the playoffs in the middle of the first game, Anthony will not need surgery on his mysteriously strained hand. "What we've been told [is] that we don't even know what surgery we would do," said Craig Breslow. And, yeah, that sentence doesn't inspire much confidence in me, either. (Sean McAdam, MassLive)
Roman Anthony having a healthy and productive 2027 season is key to the Red Sox having a productive 2027 season. But considering that the team's biggest issue is home run power, he won't be able to fix things on his own. The Red Sox know that they need to add power to the lineup, but knowing something and doing something are two different things. "Despite identifying power as a priority entering last offseason, the Red Sox' lineup took a step backward. In 2025, the Sox hit 186 homers (15th in MLB), had a .324 on-base percentage (eighth), and a .421 slugging percentage (ninth). This year, the Red Sox hit 163 homers (26th), had a .319 OBP (12th), and slugged .398 (20th)." (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)
But maybe they already have some more power in the organization in the form of Curtis Mead, whom the Red Sox appear to be penciling in at second base as they head into the offseason. "He was acquired for a reason. You see the numbers that kind of project at least toward a 30-home run season. And adding that, we were really excited about that," said Chad Tracy. (Chris Cotillo, MassLive)
The Sox best source of power in 2026, Willson Contreras, didn't sound too happy the last time he spoke to the media, following the Sox' embarrassing exit from the playoffs. But the Sox brass is confident they smoothed things over with the slugger after Tracy and Breslow met with him for over two hours on Sunday. "We actually had a great conversation, Trace and I, with Willson," Breslow said. "Many of those [details] I will keep private just to protect or just to kind of preserve the relationship that we have. But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things. And Willson would be the right person to ask directly, but he spoke very, very highly of his time here, how much he's looking forward to 2027, and the way that he and his family appreciated the Red Sox." (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
The source of Contreras' unhappiness seemed to primarily be the early hook Tracy employed in removing Sonny Gray from Game 2 against the Yankees, a decision that Tracy is owning. "I do trust Sonny Gray," Tracy said. "I do trust the guys in the bullpen as well. So again, I think the easiest way to say is it was my call. It's my decision. It went south. I think the biggest thing for me coming into this was maybe dispelling any notion of people thinking that decisions get made prior to the game or with a piece of paper or with any computer. If I can do anything just to dispel that, say, those decisions are always going to fall on me." (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
At least Contreras can comfort himself with the fact that he's a finalist for the Hank Aaron Award. The award, given to the player who had the most outstanding offensive season is, for some bizarre reason, voted on by the fans. So if you want to throw some love Willson's way, you can cast your ballot online. (MLB.com)

Red Sox already have clear 2027 plan for Curtis Mead originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox made an in-season trade for more right-handed hitting help.
They acquired infielder Curtis Mead from the Washington Nationals in exchange for left-hander Connelly Early.
Early made just one appearance with the Nationals, and Mead had just two plate appearances with the Red Sox before suffering an injury.
Mead suffered a broken wrist on a hit-by-pitch from Athletics right-hander Jack Perkins. He missed the rest of the regular season and was activated to replace Roman Anthony in the Wild Card Series.
However, manager Chad Tracy never used Mead off the bench in the postseason.
Still, the Red Sox may have him as their full-time second baseman in 2027, Tracy told reporters, including The Boston Globe's Tim Healey.
"He was acquired for a reason. You see the numbers that kind of project at least toward a 30-home run season. And adding that, we were really excited about that," Tracy told Healey.
In 88 games with the Nationals, Mead hit .253/.353/.498 with 17 home runs and a .851 OPS.
MORE: How Randal Grichuk has been a 'godsend' for the White Sox after Yankees release
Before 2026, Mead combined to hit just four homers in 152 games with the Tampa Bay Rays and Chicago White Sox.
The White Sox designated the 25-year-old for assignment at the end of spring training.
Now, the Red Sox sound fairly confident that Mead will have a strong opportunity to win the second base job at next year's spring training.

item.content:encoded:
Craig Breslow surveyed the playoff field and reached an obvious conclusion about a path for improving the Red Sox.
“It would be fair to look at some of those other teams to say that they hit the ball out of the park a little bit more than we do,” said the Sox’ chief baseball officer. “It doesn’t really matter how you score, but in the postseason, a lot of runs come via the home run because the pitching is so dominant. So I think that’s a consideration.”
The assessment certainly would have been appropriate at the Red Sox’ end-of-year news conference at Fenway Park on Monday, five days after the team got bounced from the playoffs in two games by the Yankees while managing a total of two runs. But Breslow’s observation was actually offered one year earlier, in the days after the Sox were knocked out of the 2025 Wild Card Series by the Yankees.
Despite identifying power as a priority entering last offseason, the Red Sox lineup took a step backward. In 2025, the Sox hit 186 homers (15th in MLB), had a .324 on-base percentage (eighth), and a .421 slugging percentage (ninth). This year, the Red Sox hit 163 homers (26th), had a .319 OBP (12th), and slugged .398 (20th).
Caveats are in order. The loss of Trevor Story and Roman Anthony for the majority of the year removed two batters capable of driving the ball out of the park. One of the players brought in to offset their absences, Curtis Mead, made just two plate appearances following a July trade with the Nationals before suffering a broken wrist when getting hit by a pitch.
Even with those losses, the Sox’ power deficiency was subject to exaggeration. Fenway Park played as a graveyard for power for much of the year. On the road, the Sox hit 87 homers — tied for 21st in the big leagues and well ahead of the bottom-ranked team in that category, the best-in-baseball Brewers (63). From July 1, the Sox ranked roughly in the middle of the pack in slugging and homers per game.
Still, the Sox didn’t have the depth of power to reliably outslug opponents — especially against playoff-caliber power pitching. The team went deep just 26 times against 95-plus-mile-per-hour pitches, tied for fourth fewest in the big leagues.
On Monday, Breslow — while identifying strengths in the rotation and bullpen, as well as infield and outfield defense — didn’t pretend otherwise.
“Our offense was inconsistent,” Breslow said. “We got on base at a decent clip, but we didn’t really slug. We didn’t hit a ton of home runs. I’m not sure that we took advantage of the unique venue that that we play in. Naturally, we’re going to spend some time thinking about how we improve our offense, and particularly how we build a roster that can thrive at Fenway Park.”
The quick ejection from the postseason — when the Sox allowed four homers to the Yankees, while hitting just two — further reinforced the point, and underscored the biggest lever to pull as the team looks to build a club capable of competing deeper into the playoffs.
“When you get beat in the lopsided manner that we did [in the playoffs], I think we have to evaluate, how do we improve our offense? How do we particularly improve our offense against elite pitching?” Breslow said. “We’re very familiar with our offensive production against pitchers that throw 95-plus and 97-plus (m.p.h.), and I think there are ways to train that. I also think that we have to be aware of roster construction and making sure that we have a resilient offense.”
Beyond the team’s efforts to help develop more power among returning players (while also contemplating the potential impact of Franklin Arias, whose developmental jump has evaluators forecasting him as a potential 15-20 homer hitter), the task of upgrading the offense is different than a year ago.
After the 2025 season, the free agent market featured several top- or middle-of-the-order threats, notably Alex Bregman, Pete Alonso, and Kyle Schwarber. The Sox did trade for a lineup centerpiece in Willson Contreras, but didn’t manage to add a second slugger (with Bregman the most notable near miss).
This year’s free agent class is thinner, with righthanded hitting outfielders Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, longtime Sox tormenter Brandon Lowe (a lefthanded hitting second baseman), and Nippon Pro Baseball star Teruaki Sato (expected to be posted this offseason) the best power bats on the market.
Those modest options likely explain why the Sox were so aggressive leading up to the trade deadline, not only trading for Mead and Adley Rutschman but making unsuccessful pushes for shortstops Otto Lopez of the Marlins (.396 average against 95-plus-m.p.h. pitches, best among hitters who saw at least 250 such pitches) and Zach Neto of the Angels (.489 slugging against 95-plus, 40th in MLB).
The extent of the midyear effort to upgrade the lineup served as a tell about the team’s offseason focus. There’s little question that power — particularly righthanded pull hitters who can handle velocity with a chance to mash at Fenway — once again offers the biggest potential upgrade. Breslow and the Sox now have an offseason to show whether they can achieve it.

Since aggravating his previous sprain while suffering additional injuries during Game 1 last week, Roman Anthony has had several follow-up appointments and undergone a fresh round of imaging on his right hand.
Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said based on those visits, the expectation is Anthony won’t need surgery.
“At this point it doesn’t seem that there’s any type of surgical intervention and rest is likely the best path for recovery,” Breslow said.
Anthony’s health and the handling of his injury was a consistent focus of the hourlong press conference, with the club’s leaders pressed on whether they knew he was playing through pain, if it would have made sense to undergo additional imaging before he was activated to weigh the risk of a recurrence and if the club is concerned the injury could become a chronic problem.
Over the course of the session Breslow defended the club’s process, saying everyone was on the same page throughout the summer.
“I think we had a pretty good understanding of what the diagnosis was and that Roman was very confident he could contribute, and over the course of a game there would be a swing or two that might give him he’d describe it as a bit of a zinger, and a few seconds later that feeling would subside,” Breslow said. “We wanted to balance Roman’s desire to get on the field and compete and his ability to help us win games with making sure we were doing the medically responsible thing and not trying to put him in any greater danger.”
Breslow added later that there is a big difference between rest during the season while trying to get back and perform and rest in the offseason when you can truly shut it down and allow your body to recover.
As far as other Red Sox injuries are concerned, Breslow said third baseman Caleb Durbin’s pinky is still being evaluated and it remains undetermined if he’ll need surgery.
Garrett Crochet, who missed most of the season with a left shoulder injury, came out of his Wednesday outing feeling good and is positioned for a full healthy offseason. Breslow was asked for clarity on the specific nature of his injury, which has never been disclosed beyond “left shoulder inflammation,” but did not offer a formal diagnosis.
“The imaging that we got revealed some irritation and strain to the shoulder,” Breslow said. “But as we started to peel back the layers it made more and more sense to make sure we were getting this right for the long term as opposed to just getting him back on the field as quickly as we could.”
Extra innings
Breslow confirmed that Aroldis Chapman passed his physical, formally triggering his $13 million vesting option for next season. Breslow said the team hasn’t made a decision on Garrett Whitlock’s $8.25 million club option for 2027. … Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said the club hasn’t made a decision on any of the coaches who were brought up midseason and that a decision on their futures will be made in the coming days. … While Tracy stopped short of declaring Curtis Mead the club’s starting second baseman in 2027, he said that is “broadly our plan.”

BOSTON — The Red Sox' 2026 season was strikingly similar to that of the 2025 season. For the second straight season, the team finished third in its division, accumulated a win total in the upper 80s, and got eliminated by the New York Yankees in the wild card round.
So maybe it shouldn't be much of a surprise that the team's chief baseball officer, Craig Breslow, identified the same offseason priority as (almost exactly) a year ago.
"We're in the initial stages of evaluating the season and thinking about our approach to 2027," said Breslow, "but it's not hard to look at the composition of our roster and recognize our starting pitching was consistently very good. I think by a handful of metrics, I think we had the best bullpen in baseball and the best outfield defense in baseball and an infield defense that showed marked improvement relative to the last few years.
"Our offense was inconsistent. We got on base at a decent clip but we didn't really slug (.398, 20th in MLB), didn't hit a ton of home runs (163, 26th) and I'm not sure that we took advantage of the unique venue that we play in. So naturally, we're going to spend some time thinking about how we can improve our offense, particularly how we build a roster that can thrive at Fenway Park."
Indeed, the Red Sox were just 18th in runs scored at home this past season.
Breslow expressed hope that the Sox could see significant jumps in the power department from a number of players just now entering their prime — Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu and Caleb Durbin included – while anticipating a full season from Curtis Mead, who was sidelined for more than two months after being injured in his second at-bat with the Sox.
"And also we're going to have to look at what may be available that's not currently on the roster," Breslow said, "and figure out if there's an opportunity down that path as well."
Breslow said much of the same thing after last season, while making the observation that home runs were the quickest and most efficient way to score runs, and noting that home runs become even more valuable in the postseason. A year ago, teams out-homering opponents were 30-5 in the postseason, and the same pattern is already evident this fall.
The Sox acquired their one major offensive upgrade last winter by trading for first baseman Willson Contreras, and that move paid off handsomely. Contreras enjoyed the best year of his career, leading the team in homers, RBI and OPS. He also hit one of two homers the team managed in its brief postseason.
But clearly, more is now needed.
"There are a lot of reasons to believe the existing offense should be better in 2027," said Breslow. "But we're also going to do everything we can to improve beyond that."
The problem, in part, is that the free agent market is a relatively thin one when it comes to run producers. Last year, Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso headed the free agent class; this year, the two best offensive players appear to be Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, neither of whom has that kind of power ceiling.
Another issue: should the Sox acquire another bat, where does that fit into the lineup? The team is currently set at catcher (Adley Rutschman), first (Contreras), second (Mead), shortstop (Trevor Story), third base (Durbin) and the outfield is deep with Rafaela, Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran. There could be a DH opening, but it's possible either Anthony or Duran could fill that.
"It can be a bit of a challenge when you kind of go around (the field) and say, 'We think this player is very good, this player is very good and this player is very good,'" said Breslow, "and we think that there's another step forward for them to take. Sometimes that improvement comes from taking a good player and turning them into a great player. That can be internal development or adding players to the organization who are currently out here right now."
This offseason will offer plenty of variables, not the least of which is the looming Dec. 1 lockout and the uncertainty surrounding what a new collective bargaining agreement might bring.
That could mean a busy November as teams rush to get trades or signings done before the sport closes down – or that same flurry might be postponed until a new CBA is agreed upon.
One thing, however, remains clear: the Red Sox, as currently constituted, aren't good enough offensively. And unless they want a third straight winter in which they pursue improvements, that has to be addressed.

item.content:encoded:
After playing through pain upon returning from the injured list, Red Sox outfielder Roman Anthony will not need surgery to fix his right hand/wrist, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said Monday.
Instead, the Sox plan to simply have him rest — really, truly rest, in a way that he did not when trying to return during this season.
“My understanding is that there’s no surgical intervention at this point, that is planned or that merits consideration,” Breslow said at Fenway Park, during the club’s end-of-season news conference. “What we’ve been told [is] that we don’t even know what surgery we would do.”
Breslow noted that the Red Sox are “still collecting information” on Anthony, who missed most of the season because of a partially torn ligament in his right ring finger, returned in late August, and dealt with a recurrence of that as well as other hand issues in the first of the Sox’ two postseason games.
The difference moving forward versus Anthony’s summer recovery revolves around urgency.
When trying to get better, Anthony’s ostensible rest included “trying to do everything possible to get back on the field,” Breslow said.
“When he felt comfortable and confident that he could help contribute, he pushed to get back on the field,” Breslow said. “And so he was trying to swing and he was doing tee work and dry swings as soon as he could, and a couple of times he tried and had to take a step back and would try again.”
Now, with no games for six months, there is no such pressure. The offseason provides “this window to rest it completely and make sure we don’t progress to step two until we’re complete,” Breslow said.
As for Anthony playing through pain over the month or so after he returned: The Red Sox knew that once or twice per game, he would experience a “zinger” after swinging, Breslow said, but that discomfort subsided within seconds.
When the pain became unbearable last week, Anthony was done.
“From the standpoint of, did we have a pretty good understanding of what we thought was going on, and was there kind of alignment and everyone on board with the plan? The answer is yes,” Breslow said. “Roman deserves a ton of credit for doing everything he possibly could to get back on the field. … Rest is likely the best path to recovery.”
Chapman locked up
Closer Aroldis Chapman passed his end-of-season physical, triggering his vesting option for 2027, Breslow said. He is due to make $13 million next year as part of the extension he signed in August 2025.
Breslow said the Sox have not decided on Garrett Whitlock’s $8.25 million team option for next season. They have until early November to make that official.
Wait and see for Durbin
The Red Sox don’t know yet whether Caleb Durbin will need surgery to pair his injured left pinkie finger.
“He’s had some initial appointments. He’ll have some follow-up appointments,” Breslow said. “He deserves a ton of credit for what he played through.”
Varitek update
In April, during the coaching staff overhaul, the Red Sox said Jason Varitek would be reassigned within the organization.
For now, though, he is not with the Red Sox in any capacity, team president Sam Kennedy said.
“We’ve connected with each other, but we’ve got no update on that,” Kennedy said. “Look forward to continuing dialogue as we go forward.”
Coaching continuity?
Among the unresolved loose ends in the first week of the offseason: The Red Sox are not ready to reveal the fate of the members of the makeshift coaching staff, thrown together in late April after the firing of Alex Cora.
Manager Chad Tracy is here to stay, having received a three-year contract last month. Those on his staff remain in flux.
“We’re going to continue to talk about that in the coming days,” Tracy said.
Breslow did highlight his satisfaction with the hitting staff: lead hitting coach John Soteropulos (elevated from assistant hitting coach after one month in that role), interim hitting coach Collin Hetzler, interim hitting coach Nelson Paulino, and interim hitting assistant Jack Simonetty.
“We’re confident in the job that John and the hitting group did and confident, I think, in their development backgrounds to be able to continue to push these players,” Breslow said.
Checking on Crochet
Garrett Crochet was among the Red Sox still in town as of Monday, Breslow said, and was due for one last “follow-up” with the medical staff. Breslow noted that after missing five months because of a left shoulder injury, Crochet was “feeling pretty good” in the days after pitching in the Sox’ last game Wednesday and will “go into the offseason full healthy.” … The Red Sox have Curtis Mead penciled in as the second baseman heading into 2027. “That would be, I would say, broadly our plan,” Tracy said. “He was acquired for a reason. You see the numbers that kind of project at least toward a 30-home run season. And adding that, we were really excited about that.” After being acquired from the Nationals, Mead got hit by a pitch and fractured his left wrist in his first game with the Sox … Kennedy, summing up the season: “As painful as the first half of the season was, and as sort of magical and historic as the second half of the summer became, the way it ended Wednesday night in New York was painful and deeply disappointing.”

The Wild Card series against the Yankees was probably the worst way for the 2026 season to end. Everything that was a problem at any point - struggles to score runs, the bullpen, injuries - all happened at the same time and within a matter of minutes. Two games in a row ended the Red Sox season. This wasn’t the plan. As all the Sox players returned from the WBC to Fort Myers, many riding hot streaks, this looked like a team ready to rocket. Yes, there were questions entering the season. But there were answers that hadn’t been fully formed yet.
After the 2025 season, the Sox were desperate for infield help. Trevor Story, not a guarantee of health or success himself, since arriving in Boston, was coming off a tremendous year, his best for the Red Sox. The rest of the infield was a question mark. Third base was more-or-less vacant after Alex Bregman opted out. Second base was going to be a battle with the future potential of Marcelo Mayer as a leading contestant. First base? Triston Casas? Maybe? Catcher, using the more generous definition of infield, was a tandem based on Carlos Narváez hitting in 2025 and Connor Wong, who couldn’t hit at all. There were at least two guys, which was more than could be said about first base.
Craig Breslow looked at the free agent market. He looked at the trade market. He looked at his own farm system. And in two phases he built the roster that he would live or die with.
We know about phase one. Caleb Durbin was acquired from the Milwaukee Brewers. Willson Contreras was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals. Isaiah Kiner-Falefa was signed to platoon (kinda) with Mayer.
On the free agent market, the Red Sox went in the opposite direction. The promise/hope was two bats. And they passed on Pete Alonso, Alex Bregman, Bo Bichette etc. Aside from Contreras there were no big bats.
What Durbin would share with Willson, besides become Mini Bowser to his Bowser, was control. Contreras was guaranteed to be in town through 2027 with an option for 2028. Durbin will not hit free agency until the 2030s. The same with Mayer. Ranger Suarez, on the other side of the ball, also was signed long-term.
As it would turn out Willson Contreras would not even sniff competition from Triston Casas, who would face a series of injuries that would cost him the season. Not that anyone was worried about having too many first basemen. Caleb Durbin would start off slow with the bat, glacial even, but provide solid defense. He’d go on to set a new career high in home runs while, likely, competing for a Gold Glove.
Marcelo Mayer would underperform and then get hurt. Carlos Narváez would revert to his reputation as a bat-second player. While Connor Wong would provide some offense in a bounce-back season, the catcher tandem as a whole was underwater.
Phase two would be at the deadline. With Durbin rounding into form as The Durbinator, Breslow and his team set their sights on second base and catcher. Turning Connelly Early into Curtis Mead gave them another second baseman with control for years to come. And while the sample size is small, Mead hit 17 home runs in just 87 games. Adding a 30-homer threat to second base would be a tremendous pillar of the offense. Mayer would be traded separately, Mead would get hurt, but the plan was in place.
Similarly, the massive all-in prospect trade for Adley Rutschman was for 2026 and 2027. Connor Wong isn’t a free agent until after the 2028 season so catcher is set for another year and they have time to evaluate Rutschman or find a replacement before 2028. For Breslow’s plan through this summer, when he didn’t know he’d be extended, that’s all that mattered. Build then best team for what could be his last season if they struggled.
Entering 2027 the Red Sox have two catchers. They have an entire starting infield, plus top prospect Franklin Arias. They have Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Wilyer Abreu (plus control of Jarren Duran, and Masataka Yoshida, and Kristian Campbell) in the outfield.
The rotation has Payton Tolle, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, and Jake Bennett. Boston holds an option on Sonny Gray that he can opt out of, but potentially the entire rotation is headed back for 2027. Starters 6-10 might be a concern, but for a healthy Opening Day major league roster, Breslow took care of that already.
We never actually got to see this team assembled together in 2026. Even if Curtis Mead came into the last game of the season while Garrett Crochet was on the mound, Roman was out. This year, unless there is a big trade to accommodate a move, the Hot Stove season won’t be the same. The roster is basically set. Did Breslow see the lockout as an obstacle? Maybe! He might have been thinking that teams would scramble to make moves before and after and he’d be set. For a team that was seeing it’s window open in 2025, it seems too intentional to put together the whole thing one year in with really only the Story to Arias transition as a big roster move to facilitate.
The performance of the team in 2026 was up and down, but overall we saw a number of good years from this group - Tolle, Abreu, Contreras, Rafaela, and Durbin all provide reasons to be optimistic. Roman Anthony had a good run around the hand injury. Six months off sure would be nice to let that heal. There’s reason to think 2027 can be fun. Maybe distributed a little better too.
Your Opening Day 2027 Boston Red Sox:
C: Rutschman, Wong
1: Contreras
2B: Mead, Sogard
SS: Story, Arias
3B: Durbin

As paintul as it is to lose to the New York Yankees in the playoffs (for the second year in a row, no less), it hurts more to know that the Boston Red Sox's loss was more self-inflicted than anything.
Boston's offense fell apart in September and the complete lack of momentum cursed it when it mattered. Pitching has been the Sox's single-biggest strength all season but Chad Tracy trusted the wrong arms at the wrong times. The moves could've cost the Red Sox any chance they had at a reunion with impending free agent Sonny Gray, who was vocal about his disappointment following his 4.2 inning outing.
“I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact,” Gray said. “I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am, and yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys, and they felt the same way."
The veteran has recently dropped hints that he might retire after this season, but after the Sox's loss he changed his tune, saying he's "got a lot of baseball left in [him]." Despite Boston's need for a right-handed pitcher next season, it's hard to foresee a reunion with Gray now.
The Sox have another impending free agent who likely won't want to come back after some explosive postgame comments, as well as some other players who could be moved after a disappointing loss.
Sonny Gray and 3 other Red Sox who won't be back after embarrassing Yankees series
Isiah Kiner-Falefa
Isiah Kiner-Falefa is yet another veteran who came to the Red Sox organization and revealed issues with the club's internal workings. Before the Red Sox went off on their tear over the summer, Kiner-Falefa called out some outside distractions that kept them from performing. He called the Sox's Wild Card loss "unacceptable" after Game 2.
Falefa didn't appear in the Wild Card series against the Yankees and he doesn't have a place in the Red Sox's infield next year — Trevor Story is under contract for one more season, Franklin Arias should be in the big leagues on Opening Day, Curtis Mead should be healthy and Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler will be options off the bench. But Kiner-Falefa has also called out the behind-the-scenes drama in the Red Sox organization and most likely prefers to play for a better-run team next year.
Patrick Sandoval
Patrick Sandoval didn't make the Red Sox's Wild Card roster, and there's a good reason for it. The lefty posted a 5.12 ERA and a 1.68 WHIP over 70.1 innings this year. He struggled in August and September with a 5.79 ERA between the two months. Seven of his eight decisions were losses.
The Red Sox certainly don't need another lefty starter in their rotation given the group they'll carry into next season. Boston's post-UCL surgery rebound projects have largely been unsuccessful and Sandoval did not change that.
Jarren Duran
The Red Sox hoped to rely on Jarren Duran as a veteran presence and an offensive threat this season and he was neither. He finished the season with a .207/.266/.361 slash line and 165 strikeouts in 151 games, the worst marks of his career so far.
Boston was already past the point of getting a good trade return for Duran last season, but the return doesn't matter at this point. The Red Sox need right-handed power and consistency and it makes the most sense to add it in the outfield.

The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now.
Essentially all of last offseason was spent with the premise that the Red Sox had too many outfielders and that one was bound to get traded.
That never came to fruition, though, and so Duran remained in Boston for the 2026 season.
He struggled mightily, batting just .207 with limited power, and so questions will arise again.
The Red Sox still have the same amount of outfielders. Duran might not be worth as much, but he also might not be as crucial for Boston to keep around.
A year later, could a trade materialize?
That’s one question being asked as the Red Sox enter their offseason after being swept in two games in the AL Wild Card Series by the rival New York Yankees.
There are big questions for the sport of baseball to answer as a whole this winter. In Boston, though, Duran is going to be one of the biggest things to solve, one way or another.
Jarren Duran Trade Plans
ESPN’s David Schoenfield wrote about this question almost immediately following the Red Sox season ending, and he seems to arrive at the conclusion that a trade could definitely be coming.
“That leaves trading Duran on the agenda,” Schoenfield writes. “Roman Anthony’s nearly four-month stint on the IL meant the four-outfielders-for-three-positions problem never actually turned into a problem, but after hitting just .207/.266/.361, Duran is clearly fourth on the depth chart. His trade value took a nosedive, but he still somehow has two years left of team control, and the Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.”
There is certainly value for an acquiring team in the fact that Duran still has two more years under contract. Especially considering what a shortened season might do to player value, a team knowing it would also have Duran for 2028 could be appealing to anyone who still believes in his talent.
There may not be a lot of suitors, but Schoenfield writes that the “Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.” It’ll just be up to Boston at that point to follow through on the deal.
Why Red Sox Offseason Might Be Slow Otherwise
Aside from Duran, Schoenfield doesn’t think Boston will be very busy. They’ve already taken care of a bunch of things.
“While the Red Sox had a revolving door at shortstop and second base in 2026 — six different players started at short and seven at second — those positions will probably be resolved in 2027 with top prospect Franklin Arias and Curtis Mead, the trade deadline acquisition the Red Sox were going to play at second base until he got injured his first game with the team,” Schoenfield writes. “Trevor Story still has one more year left on his contract, but there’s no reason he should be playing ahead of Arias next season.”
Schoenfield also references the recent trades for Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Erik Miller as limiting the need for moves, since those guys all are under contract still.
His only other question: Does Sonny Gray retire, or return, or neither? The Red Sox still have things to figure out, just maybe not as much as some years.

The worst news for Boston fans isn't that Roman Anthony is hurt. It is that the injury is worse than anyone thought. New scans revealed fresh muscle strains in his wrist alongside old damage. This changes everything for the Red Sox playoff hopes.
Scans Show Worse Damage
Anthony left Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with soreness after a checked swing. He struck out twice before getting pulled in a 9-0 loss. Manager Chad Tracy said the player was sent back to Boston for more imaging. The results were grim. "We sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist in addition to exasperating the old injuries. It's not great," Tracy told reporters, per ESPN.
This isn't a minor tweak. The 22-year-old missed 101 games earlier this year with a torn ligament in his right ring finger. He only played 55 regular season games before this latest setback. His stats dropped from a .292 average last year to .245 this season. The Red Sox signed him to a massive $130 million extension hoping for a star. Now that deal looks like a gamble on a broken body.
A Brutal Playoff Rule
There is a cruel twist in the rulebook that fans need to know. If a player gets removed from a playoff roster during a series, he cannot play in the next series either. This means Anthony won't just miss Game 2 against the Yankees. He will be ineligible for the entire ALDS if Boston advances. The team replaced Anthony on the roster with Curtis Mead, according to MLB Trade Rumors.
Tracy tried to frame it as a common issue for players coming off long layoffs. "He's obviously coming off that. You'll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it's fine, it goes away," Tracy said. But the reality is different today. "Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable," he added, per ESPN. The hope is gone. The pain is real.
The Cost of a Broken Star
The Red Sox are one loss from elimination. They need every bat they can get. Jahmai Jones is set to hit leadoff as the designated hitter. The lineup includes Adley Rutschman, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu. Sonny Gray will start on the mound against a former team. But the lineup is missing its most promising young hitter.
Anthony was supposed to be the centerpiece of the next decade. His wrist issues have already cost the team almost four months of the regular season. Now they lose him in the playoffs too. The $130 million contract is secure, but the on-field value is gone for now. Boston has to hope Mead or Seigler can step up immediately. The clock is ticking, and the scans say time is not on their side.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — When the Red Sox activated Garrett Crochet and included him on their postseason roster, they no doubt hoped that when he eventually took the mound it would be to protect a late lead and help lock down a crucial playoff win.
They didn’t have anything like the nightmare that unfolded Wednesday in mind.
Crochet finally took the mound for the first time since April 25 with the Red Sox trailing 2-1 in the sixth inning. Boston had just scored on a Willson Contreras solo homer, breaking up the club’s marathon streak of 26.2 consecutive scoreless postseason innings dating back to Game 2 of last fall’s Wild Card Series.
Even a one-run deficit felt daunting with the way the Red Sox have been hitting since the start of September, so it was incumbent on Crochet to keep the Yankees from getting any further ahead.
Things started off well enough — Crochet’s first pitch was a 97 mph sinker to Spencer Jones — but then the storybook moment fell apart.
Crochet struck Jones out with a filthy sweeper, but Adley Rutschman couldn’t handle it and Jones reached on the dropped third strike. He then stole second, took third on Rutschman’s throwing error and scored on George Lombard Jr.’s ensuing RBI single. Things snowballed from there with three straight hits, and before Crochet knew what hit him the bases were loaded with nobody out, and manager Chad Tracy was coming out to summon Garrett Whitlock to put out the fire.
Everyone came around to score, and when Cody Bellinger took Whitlock deep for a three-run home run to make it 8-1, the Red Sox were well and truly cooked en route to a season-ending 9-2 loss.
Crochet’s final line: four batters faced, four runs scored, no outs recorded.
“It sucks. Personally to think that I busted my (butt) for the past five months for it to end that way, on a personal note it’s tough,” Crochet said postgame. “I just wanted to come back and contribute to the team as best as I could and I let them down.”
In the end, Boston’s late arriving reinforcements proved too little, too late.
Even if Crochet had pitched a perfect sixth inning, it was abundantly clear throughout the series that the Yankees were the better team. Only one team’s starting pitchers worked deep into the ballgame, and only one team’s lineup consistently came through with timely hits and back-breaking home runs.
That sure wasn’t the Red Sox, so if there’s one silver lining Crochet can take away, it’s that he at least got his opportunity to turn the tide after grinding through five months of recovery and rehab from his nagging shoulder injury.
Though in the immediate aftermath, Crochet certainly didn’t feel that way.
“It was definitely nice to touch again, it’s hard to find a lot of positives to take when you don’t record an out,” Crochet said. “I felt like I was in control as much as you can be when you’re getting the (expletive) beat out of you, but at the end of the day I did what I wanted to do out there and it wasn’t good enough. That’s really all it is.”
That’s more than Curtis Mead can say.
Acquired prior to the trade deadline from the Washington Nationals in exchange for Connelly Early, Mead was brought to Boston specifically to fortify the Red Sox lineup for big games like this one. Mead suffered a fractured left wrist in his first game with the club after being hit by a pitch, but over the past week he finally turned the corner in his recovery and was activated as an injury replacement for Roman Anthony ahead of Game 2.
Prior to the game Mead spoke about how special it was getting to suit up for a playoff game, admitting that not long ago he didn’t think he’d be back in time.
“Probably two weeks ago if you asked if I thought I’d be in this position, the answer would probably be no,” Mead said. “So it’s definitely exciting.”
Mead did not appear in Wednesday’s loss, but had the Red Sox forced a decisive Game 3 there is a chance Mead might have had a chance to start, most likely as the designated hitter in Anthony’s place. Would he have fared any better than Crochet in his return? He only just faced live pitching for the first time during Monday’s team workout at Yankee Stadium, when he squared off against rookie left-hander Tyler Samaniego in a live batting practice session.
Before that, he’d just hit off the Trajekt machine — a state-of-the-art pitching machine that mimics actual big leaguers — for the first time on Saturday at Tropicana Field.
In many respects, that super accelerated ramp-up mirrored Crochet’s return to action.
Like Mead, the Red Sox ace couldn’t get back on the field until after the minor league season was over. That meant a rehab assignment wasn’t on the table, so if either of them were going to come back there was inevitably going to be some element of being tossed back into the fire.
Even for a pitcher of Crochet’s caliber, jumping right into the boiling cauldron that is Yankee Stadium a few outs from a playoff series victory was always going to be a Hail Mary.
While the Baseball Gods have answered Boston’s prayers in the postseason before, this year it just wasn’t meant to be.
“These guys grinded all year long, I think that we’re maybe a little undeserving of the fate we got but sometimes that’s the game,” Crochet said. “Sometimes it’s good, sometimes it’s (expletive), sometimes you do all the right things and it doesn’t go your way. Ultimately they executed at a higher clip than us and that’s the game.”

The Boston Red Sox replaced injured outfielder Roman Anthony on their wild-card series roster with infielder Curtis Mead on Wednesday ahead of Game 2 against the New York Yankees.
Anthony underwent imaging in Boston on Wednesday morning that displayed he had 'additional damage to some muscles' in his right hand and wrist, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said prior to Game 2 of the American League series.
Anthony had an injury to the same hand earlier this season that caused him to miss nearly four months. He returned to action Aug. 30.
Major League Baseball approved the roster change after reviewing the medical information. Anthony will be ineligible to return if the Red Sox reach the AL Division Series, but he will be eligible to play if Boston advances to the AL Championship Series.
Anthony started Tuesday's 9-0 loss in Game 1 batting leadoff as the designated hitter and struck out in both at-bats -- on checked swings -- against New York's Cam Schlittler. The hand injury flared up and he couldn't continue. Anthony was replaced by Andruw Monasterio in the sixth inning.
Tracy was unsure if the 22-year-old Anthony might require hand surgery.
'I don't know the answer to that yet,' Tracy said. 'I just know that the imaging shows more than what was originally there. So as far as what treatment plans are in the future, haven't gotten there.
'Just midday today I first found out, yeah, there's more there that we're not going to have him. We'll figure it out as we move along.'
Anthony batted .245 with five homers and 15 RBIs in 55 games.
Mead was acquired from the Washington Nationals a few days ahead of the trade deadline and sustained a broken left wrist in his first game with the team.
He was hit by a pitch from Athletics right-hander Jack Perkins in the fourth inning of his debut on July 27.
Mead, 25, hit .254 with 17 homers, 17 doubles and 48 RBIs -- all career highs - in 87 games with the Nationals before the trade.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox's Roman Anthony diagnosed with right hand strain, ineligible to return until ALCS
The Red Sox announced that Roman Anthony would not be in the Boston Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of their AL Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees on Wednesday night, a day after leaving the opener because of hand pain.
In a statement on Wednesday, the team announced that Anthony was diagnosed with a right-hand strain and was substituted off the roster.
Anthony can no longer participate in the remainder of the Wild Card Series or the American League Division Series if Boston advances.
He would be eligible to return for the American League Championship Series.
"I feel sick to my stomach. I haven't slept much. It doesn't feel real, to be honest," Anthony said Wednesday. "I been through so many emotions and feelings to get the same news again and even worse, it's hard to have an answer to anything right now."
The team announced that infielder Curtis Mead will replace Anthony on the Wild Card Series roster.
Anthony said he wasn't sure what the treatment plan would be currently to remedy his hand injury.
"Once we decided I wasn't going to play today, that's all that really mattered," Anthony said. "All that mattered was putting the team in the best situation to win."
Batting leadoff as a designated hitter in his playoff debut Tuesday, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against Cam Schlittler before getting lifted for a pinch hitter with his team trailing by two runs in the sixth inning of a 9-0 loss.
Boston manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings. The 22-year-old Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29 with an injury to the same hand.
"Unfortunately, I checked swing on my second at-bat and I knew right then and there it was time to get it looked and put somebody else in the game that would have a better chance to win," Anthony said.
“He’s obviously coming off that. You’ll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it’s fine, it goes away,” Tracy said. “Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable.”
Jahmai Jones was set to hit leadoff as the DH with the Red Sox one loss from elimination, followed in the batting order by catcher Adley Rutschman, first baseman Willson Contreras, right fielder Wilyer Abreu, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, third baseman Caleb Durbin, second baseman Nick Sogard, shortstop Trevor Story and left fielder Nate Eaton.
Sonny Gray was set to start on the mound for Boston against one of his former teams.
One of baseball’s premier prospects when he debuted last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBIs and a .735 OPS in 55 games this season.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

With Roman Anthony’s availability in doubt this postseason, the Red Sox are turning to another slugger to add pop to the lineup.
The Red Sox and MLB announced Wednesday evening that Boston completed a playoff roster substitution, with infielder/DH Curtis Mead joining the Red Sox in place of Anthony, who suffered another hand injury during Boston’s Game 1 loss to the Yankees in the Wild Card series.
It remains to be seen just how much Mead can offer a Red Sox lineup that was completely befuddled by Cam Schlittler in Game 1.
Mead — acquired by Boston in a one-for-one swap with Connelly Early as part of a trade with the Nationals in July — has not appeared in a game since July 27 after suffering a fractured wrist.
He will not be in Boston’s lineup to open a do-or-die Game 2 in the Bronx on Wednesday, but the 25-year-old Mead said that he’ll be ready to contribute if called upon during this series — likely in a pinch-hitting spot in this upcoming bout with the Yankees.
“I think I feel 100 percent,” Mead told reporters at Yankee Stadium, including MassLive’s Sean McAdam. “I feel like I’m ready however the team needs me. I’m excited to hopefully get the opportunity tonight or tomorrow.”
Despite Mead’s comments, the Red Sox infielder hasn’t had much of a ramp-up before potentially getting thrown into the middle of a high-stakes playoff game on Wednesday or Thursday.
Mead broke his wrist in his Red Sox debut, taking a fastball near his hand off a check swing in just his second plate appearance with his new team. He couldn’t take part in any rehab games before Boston’s minor-league campaigns wrapped — and only faced live BP earlier this week down in Florida.
“Obviously, it’s not ideal, right?” Mead told McAdam of his accelerated return to game action. “But I think with the injury to Roman and even Mickey [Gasper] and just some guys being banged up, I feel like in as good a spot if not better than some of those guys. So I definitely feel like I can put together some good at-bats.”
With Mead replacing Anthony on Boston’s playoff roster, Anthony will be ineligible to play until at least the ALCS — although it’s unclear if the Red Sox get that far, and whether Anthony will be cleared to play by then.
“Sore,” Tracy said of Anthony’s status on Wednesday afternoon. “He was sent back last night after leaving the game. We sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist in addition to exacerbating the old injuries. It’s not great. I know there’s enough there, and enough new stuff there, where [Anthony] is not gonna be able to play.”
Mead might be a wild card this postseason due to that injury and his limited time facing live pitching. But the young slugger was once viewed as a sizable upgrade for Boston’s lineup this summer before his untimely injury.
Mead was in the middle of a breakout season with the Nationals before arriving in Boston in July, with the Australian-born infielder batting .256 with 17 home runs, 48 RBI and an .852 OPS over 87 games in Washington.
If the Red Sox do extend their season for at least another game with a win in Game 2, Mead said that he’s not sure if he’ll be called into the lineup for a decisive Game 3 on Thursday.
“I’m not sure,” Mead told McAdam. “That’s up to [Tracy] and the coaching staff. If they asked if I would be ready, yeah, I would absolutely be ready. I think the goal is to just get through the night and then assess where we’re at tomorrow.
“Probably two weeks ago, if you had asked if I thought I’d be in this position, the answer would probably be ‘no.’ It’s definitely exciting.”

Roman Anthony out of Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of Wild Card Series
The Red Sox season will rest on the arm of starting pitcher Sonny Gray as the team takes on the New York Yankees on Wednesday in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series.
The Sox won't have the services of Roman Anthony, who appeared to reaggravate his hand injury during the team's 9-0 loss in Game 1.
"We actually sent him back to Boston last evening to get there so he could be early in the morning and re-image the hand, which shows additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. "So he's sore and obviously not in the lineup."
Anthony will be replaced on the roster by infielder Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist during his debut with the Red Sox on July 27. Anthony would eligible to return to the lineup for the American League Championship Series.
The Sox will have long odds to beat to continue their playoff run. Teams taking a 1-0 lead in a three-game wild-card series have gone on to win that series 21 out of 24 times, 17 times with a sweep.
Home teams have won all nine series in which they have won the first game.
On Tuesday, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler and the rest of the pitching staff held the Sox to just three hits.
Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle might have been the team's best player, but manager Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning of a 1-run game. Reliever Erik Miller immediately gave up a homer to Dartmouth College graduate Ben Rice, and it was all downhill from there.
On Wednesday night, Gray will pitch opposite Yankees starter Max Fried.

Batting leadoff as the Red Sox designated hitter in his playoff debut, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against before getting lifted for a pinch hitter with his team trailing 2-0 in the sixth inning. New York took a 1-0 lead in the best-of-three series with a 9-0 victory.
Manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings. The 22-year-old Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29 with an injury to the same hand. Tracy said it doesn't appear the latest injury is necessarily related, as it involves muscles in the wrist.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," Anthony told reporters on Wednesday. "Last night just felt a little more intense, little bit more harsh than past swings have and lingered a little bit longer than the ones I was used to had. So it just was super alarming and got to the point where it was tough to grip a bat."
The manager said that after the game, Anthony returned to Boston for imaging on his hand, which found "additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before."
Anthony is not in Wednesday night's lineup, when the Red Sox must win to extend their season. Jahmai Jones is leading off at DH in Anthony's absence.
Wednesday night, the team announced that infielder Curtis Mead replaced Anthony on the Wild Card roster. That means that if the Red Sox advance to the ALDS, Anthony would be out for that round as well.
One of baseball's premier prospects when he arrived in the majors last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBIs and a .735 OPS in 55 regular-season games this season.
"He's a really good player. Certainly not something we wanted to happen and having him in there is important. But can't reiterate enough, we've dealt with things like this all year. But the show goes on, you've got to play tonight and be able to win a ballgame," Tracy said.
The manager added that it is not yet known if Anthony will need surgery.
Sonny Gray is on the mound for the Red Sox in Game 2, which is scheduled to start at 8:15 p.m.

Once again, the Boston Red Sox will be without Roman Anthony for the playoffs. After being removed from the game in the sixth inning of Game 1 against the New York Yankees, the Red Sox sent him back to Boston overnight for more imaging on the hand he injured earlier in the season. The results showed aggravation of his precious injury, as well as new strains in his wrist.
Reports from the Red Sox today said that this injury will keep Anthony out for the foreseeable future. The Red Sox officially removed Anthony from the playoff roster, meaning he is done for the Wild Card and division series, at least. If he is healthy, he could be added to the ALCS roster if Boston makes it.
Because Anthony was removed due to an injury, the Red Sox are allowed to replace him on the roster. Speculation early in the day was between two players, and ultimately, the Sox chose Curtis Mead.
Red Sox hope Curtis Mead continues early season breakout to keep them alive against Yankees
The Red Sox acquired Mead a week before the trade deadline, sending back a highly touted young pitcher, Connelly Early. Mead was in the midst of a breakout season when Boston acquired him. After bouncing around a few franchises, he settled in with the Washington Nationals this season.
Mead batted .254 with an .852 OPS in 87 games with the Nationals. He logged 17 doubles, 17 home runs, and 48 RBI. He had an almost 12% walk rate with a strikeout rate under 20%; he was one of just 22 hitters with more than 300 at-bats to do that this season. While some were wary that the infielder's breakout wasn't sustainable, his underlying metrics suggested what was happening was real.
The 25-year-old was supposed to add major pop to the Sox lineup. Unfortunately, just two at-bats into his Red Sox career, he was hit on the wrist with a pitch, causing a fracture. The injury cost him the rest of the regular season. Most of Red Sox Nation assumed it was going to be a "see you next year" scenario, but he worked his way back to health, and now the team is calling on him to step in for Anthony.
Mead has not been substituted into the lineup for Game 2 of the Wild Card, and according to MassLive's Chris Cotillo the Red Sox aren't expected to add him. Although he's not in the starting nine, it's very likely Red Sox Nation will see him pinch hit in the win-or-go-home game.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The 2026 Red Sox season could come to an end on Wednesday night, but Roman Anthony’s year is already officially over.
The 22-year-old outfielder/designated hitter was not in the Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of the Wild Card round, and will be replaced on the roster by infielder Curtis Mead.
Anthony not only reaggravated the right hand injury that sidelined him for over three months of the regular season, but sustained new muscular damage in his wrist, manager Chad Tracy announced pregame.
“(Imaging) showed additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren’t there before,” Tracy said.
Tuesday’s series-opener was Anthony’s first career postseason game, as he missed last year’s Wild Card round at Yankee Stadium due to an oblique strain in early September of his rookie year. But his Game 1 as leadoff man and DH lasted all of two at-bats, both strikeouts, before Andruw Monasterio pinch-hit for him in the top of the sixth.
Anthony was not made available to the press in the visitors’ clubhouse following Tuesday night’s 9-0 Game 1 loss, and Red Sox media relations said he had already departed Yankee Stadium. Tracy explained Wednesday that they sent Anthony to Boston for testing after the previous night’s game, but that he was already on his way back to New York to be with the team for Game 2.
“He’s upset; mentally, going through it,” Tracy said of his conversations with Anthony. “It was grinding on him, for sure. He’s upset. He wants to be out there with the guys, and obviously, everything he’s gone through this year, dealing with all these different things, it’s been tough for him.”
Tracy did not have many concrete answers on next steps, after receiving the news “just midday” on Wednesday. The Sox skipper said he did not know yet if surgery is necessary, or who would replace Anthony on the roster. Speedy minor league outfielder Braiden Ward would have been a likely candidate, as he was originally with the Red Sox when they arrived in New York, but Tracy said Ward was no longer on-site.
“I just know that the imaging shows more than what was originally there,” Tracy said. “We’re trying to replace him, we have paperwork in on that (to the league office), but it’s enough there that we’re not going to have him.”
An hour later, MLB communications announced the approval of Mead as Anthony’s roster replacement.
There’s an element of brutal irony to this swap. Anthony’s hand sidelined him between May 5 and Aug. 29, and Mead has not played since suffering a wrist fracture on a hit-by-pitch in his second at-bat after the Red Sox acquired him from the Washington Nationals in late July.
But the Red Sox did not have time to dwell on any of it. Wednesday is win-or-go-home.
“Can’t reiterate enough, we’ve dealt with things like this all year,” Tracy said, “and show goes on.”

item.content:encoded:
Lost amid the embarrassing madness of Tuesday's Wild Card series opener between the Boston Red Sox and the New York Yankees was Roman Anthony being pinch-hit for midway through the game, seemingly out of nowhere. After the game, it was revealed by manager Chad Tracy that Anthony had re-aggravated the wrist injury that had kept him out for more than three months during the regular season — and that his Game 2 status was up in the air.
Well, Boston's Game 2 lineup is out, and it's safe to say the fan base won't like it, with Anthony on the bench.
Is Roman Anthony playing tonight? Red Sox's lineup gives answer
Here's a look at Boston's Anthony-less lineup against Yankees left-hander Max Fried.
| Player | Position |
|---|---|
| 1. Jahmai Jones | DH |
| 2. Adley Rutschman | C |
| 3. Willson Contreras | 1B |
| 4. Wilyer Abreu | RF |
| 5. Ceddanne Rafaela | CF |
| 6. Caleb Durbin | 3B |
| 7. Nick Sogard | 2B |
| 8. Trevor Story | SS |
| 9. Nate Eaton | LF |
Yeah, the Red Sox are going to miss Anthony dearly. Sure, there's the makings of a decent lineup here. Jahmai Jones has done nothing but crush lefties since the Red Sox acquired him. Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras are proven stars. Wilyer Abreu has broken out against left-handers this season, in particular. Ceddanne Rafaela is having his best offensive year. Still, there's no replacing Anthony.
He only appeared in 55 regular-season games and didn't look great in his two at-bats on Tuesday, but nobody in Boston's organization has a higher ceiling than Anthony. Being without him makes the already daunting challenge of rebounding from an 0-1 deficit in the best-of-three series that much more difficult.
Red Sox's growing injury report makes it tougher to believe in dream run
What makes Anthony's injury that much more difficult is that he's far from the only one. The Red Sox have a slew of notables on the IL, and that's making achieving their ultimate gol tough to believe in.
| Player | Position | Injury | Return |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mickey Gasper | C/INF | Right biceps strain | 2027 |
| Tyron Guerrero | RHP | Right shoulder strain | 2027 |
| Eli White | INF/OF | Ligament damage in right foot | 2027 |
| Curtis Mead | INF | Left wrist fracture | Postseason or 2027 |
| Kutter Crawford | RHP | Right flexor irritation | 2027 |
| Johan Oviedo | RHP | Right flexor strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Anthony Siegler | INF | Right wrist discomfort | Postseason or 2027 |
| Justin Slaten | RHP | Right elbow inflammation | 2027 |
| Masataka Yoshida | DH | Left hamstring strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Triston Casas | 1B | Left abdominal strain | 2027 |
The list is lengthy and littered with quality talent. Lineup-wise, the Red Sox sure could use Mickey Gasper, who was one of their hottest hitters before suffering his injury, right about now. They could also use Curtis Mead, a player who crushes left-handed pitching. Even Masataka Yoshida's bat would really come in handy with Anthony out.
Pitching-wise, Boston's depth has taken a hit. Tyron Guerrero and Justin Slaten are two of the most important members of their bullpen, and perhaps they would've been able to keep the game closer on Tuesday had they been healthy. Guys like Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo are proven back-end starters who could've eaten innings this October.
Perhaps the Red Sox can get Mead and a few others back if they can get past the Yankees, but with Anthony now joining the laundry list of injured players, it's getting tough to believe in them making a comeback.

item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

Throughout the season, first baseman Willson Contreras has been the emotional heart for the Boston Red Sox. However, he largely hasn’t been able to play in the month of September due to injuries.
He spent time on the IL due to a hamstring injury. That had been bugging him for some time, and the Red Sox wanted him to reset and get healthy for the postseason. He did, but almost as soon as he came back, he was hit in the right hand by a pitch. That forced Contreras to miss about a week and a half before DHing in the final game of the season on Sunday.
Boston Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy on Willson Contreras in the Playoffs
In the end, Willson Contreras had just two at-bats on Sunday. He’d go 0-2 with a strikeout before Jahmai Jones came in to pinch-hit for him.
It was a small sample size, but it was another emotional boost that Contreras could provide the Red Sox. The postseason is here and he’s healthy enough to play. Better than that, after the game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy confirmed that he should be available for the Wild Card Round in the postseason.
“He was okay,” Tracy said. “Took the first one [at-bat]. Took the second one. Had a pretty good at-bat. Hit the ball hard to third and he was good. So, I got him out of there… Should be [good to go].
Getting hit on the hand is risky, with plenty of smaller bones to break. Luckily, X-Rays showed that Contreras avoided that, and was just dealing with bad swelling that made it hard to swing a bat. He had previously been anxious about his availability for the postseason when describing it as a bone bruise.
“Yeah, there’s no fracture or anything,” Contreras said. “I had a CT scan yesterday just to make sure that I don’t have any fracture, and it didn’t show any fracture. At this point, still inflammation and a bone bruise.”
This comes at a time when the Red Sox have been desperately trying to get healthy. Players like Adley Rutschman and Caleb Durbin are banged up but playing through it. Others, like Ceddanne Rafaela and Curtis Mead, have needed to spend time on the IL.
Now, the Red Sox will turn their attention ahead to the New York Yankees. The American League Wild Card Series will begin on Tuesday, September 29th in the Bronx. First pitch is scheduled for 8:00 p.m. EST.
It’s Been a Career Season for Contreras
The frustrating part of the injuries for Contreras, other than that it could cost him time in the postseason, is that this has been a career season for him. This comes in his first year with the Red Sox as he’s brought a swing made for Fenway Park to Boston.
He’s hitting .276 with a .905 OPS. Contreras also has 27 home runs and 81 RBIs. That’s in a 129 game effort, and amounted to 4.5 WAR, per Baseball Reference.
Statistically, it’s Contreras’ best season. His previous high for WAR was 4.2 back in 2021. Otherwise, he hadn’t cracked that 4.0 WAR mark before. That was also a new single-season high for home runs and RBIs in his career. So, maybe it shouldn’t be a surprise that’s a career-record for OPS in a season, too.
The Red Sox need that version of Contreras in the postseason. Without him, they’re going to be looking far and wide for their power in the lineup.

The Boston Red Sox traded Connelly Early to the Washington Nationals on July 26 in exchange for infielder Curtis Mead. The Red Sox needed a bat for the playoff push. The Nationals got a young arm to build around.
Two months later, the two players have a combined two games for their teams. Early went on the injured list before the trade with left elbow inflammation. Mead fractured his left wrist in his first game after arriving in Boston.
On Saturday, Easrly finally made his first start for Washington.
Early’s Nationals Debut
Early started against the New York Mets on Saturday and threw three scoreless innings in what Washington limited to a 34-pitch outing. He allowed one hit and struck out one. His fastball touched 94.2 mph multiple times during the outing, right in line with the velocity he carried as a healthy member of the Red Sox rotation.
The workload was intentionally short given the nature of his throwing arm injury, but Early left the mound pleased with what he delivered.
“It ended up probably my cleanest three innings of the season,” Early said, per MLB.com’s Jessica Camerato.
Nationals manager Blake Butera made clear what the organization sees in Early going forward.
“He’s going to be a huge, huge part of this,” Butera said.
What the Red Sox Traded Away
Early was one of the more promising young arms in Boston’s system before the deal. The left-hander won the fifth-starter job in spring training and posted 93 strikeouts and a 3.44 ERA across 91⅔ innings before elbow inflammation shut him down on July 1.
His final start as a Red Sox came against Washington. Now he pitches for them.
Early’s path to Saturday’s debut was not smooth. After the trade, he suffered a setback in his recovery that raised concerns about whether he would pitch again in 2026. He made it back with just enough time to get one start in before the regular season ends.
The fastball sat where it needed to. The command was there. For a pitcher who had not thrown in a game since June 30, the results could not have been much cleaner.
Where the Trade Stands Now
The Red Sox made the deal to get Mead’s bat into the lineup for the stretch run. That has not happened.
Mead fractured his wrist almost immediately after arriving and has spent nearly his entire time in Boston on the injured list. He took batting practice off a machine on Friday and traveled to Fort Myers for further workouts, but his availability for the Wild Card Series remains uncertain.
Meanwhile, Early just showed Washington what he can do when healthy. The Nationals are not contending this year, but they now have a left-hander with front-of-the-rotation upside under club control for years to come.
The trade may still work out for the Red Sox if Mead gets healthy and contributes in October or beyond. But right now, the player Boston gave up is the one making strides.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Mead’s bat, when healthy, addresses a real need for Boston. But the early returns have favored Washington. Early looked like the pitcher the Red Sox developed, and the Nationals are already talking about him as a cornerstone.
The Red Sox will evaluate this deal over years, not months. For now, they are focused on Tuesday and the Wild Card Series. Whether Mead is part of that remains to be seen.

The Boston Red Sox are just a few days away from kicking off a three-game wild-card series against the New York Yankees on the road for the second straight season.
Boston and New York will begin the postseason run on Sep. 29. As the regular season has wrapped up, the biggest red flag for the Red Sox has been their sluggish offense. Throughout the month of September, Boston's offense has been one of the worst in the league. In fact, Boston has scored the fewest runs in baseball in September with just 69 in 23 games. But there is a bright spot, Boston fans. Roman Anthony is starting to look like himself at the plate at the perfect time.
Since Sep. 18, Anthony has batted .357 (10-for-28) with one homer, four doubles and a triple in seven games played. That's the type of production that is going to get the offense back on track. With Willson Contreras up in the air with his hand sore after getting hit by a pitch and Mickey Gasper also getting hurt, Boston needs guys to step up right now. The lights are starting to get bright. Boston has just one more regular season game left on Sunday before the full focus will turn to the playoffs.
Roman Anthony Is Getting Hot
If the Red Sox are going to make a run, they're going to need a lot from Anthony. When healthy, the Red Sox have arguably the deepest lineup in the American League playoffs, but will they actually find a way to get healthy? That's the question. Again, Contreras is up in the air. Gasper hurt his bicep on Friday and the club didn't give an optimistic update in the aftermath. Curtis Mead is on the shelf right now, although he is working his way back. Ceddanne Rafaela missed some time. Masataka Yoshida is on the Injured List as well, and the list goes on and on.
Boston isn't entering the playoffs at full strength, so it needs the guys who are healthy to carry the load to give this club enough time to advance and get closer to full strength. There isn't a guy in the lineup who moves the needle more than Anthony when he's rolling. We've started to see signs of that. If you have Anthony consistently getting on base at the top of the order, there's still enough talent behind him to get some runs in.
Boston's biggest strength is the pitching. The rotation and bullpen have carried the load all season. If they keep pitching as they have, Boston won't need many runs to win games. If Anthony can keep up his recent hot streak, that could be enough to help push Boston forward. He's that impactful.

The Boston Red Sox on September 24 dodged a bullet with a second potential Ceddanne Rafaela injury, but got a devastating Willson Contreras update. The veteran is still feeling pain while swinging after he was hit on his right hand by a pitch and he called into question his availability for the postseason.
The Red Sox also got an update on a long shot return candidate that could keep some hope alive. Trade deadline acquisition Curtis Mead on Friday will take batting practice off a pitching machine, according to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe (subscription required).
Mead will head to Fort Myers to join a number of players the Red Sox already have there, and Garrett Crochet will join him. Healey reports that Mead might take more batting practice off Crochet on Saturday.
The Red Sox have not formally ruled out activating Mead before the Wild Card round, which begins on September 29. It will be a close call, but there is still a slight chance that Mead could join the team before the first playoff series.
There's still a slim chance Curtis Mead could be ready for Red Sox's Wild Card series
The Red Sox dealt for Mead at the trade deadline to bring some power to their infield. The second baseman slashed .254/.352/.500 with 17 doubles and 17 home runs with the Washington Nationals. He's been on the injured list healing a fractured wrist after two at-bats in a Red Sox uniform. He hasn't appeared in a game since July 27.
There is some risk to rushing Mead back into action since he hasn't played in so long. If he does return, he'll do so without a rehab assignment because the WooSox's season has been over since September 19. If Mead isn't properly warmed up, a postseason rotation will be a rude awakening.
Still, the Red Sox's offense needs a serious lift, and even the possibility that Mead could help might be motivation enough for them to add him to the playoff roster. Boston's bats have slumped hard in September — the Red Sox have the second-lowest batting average (.221) and OPS (.656) this month and they won't get past the New York Yankees' pitching staff in that state.
Red Sox fans shouldn't get their hopes up about Mead's return. Even though he hasn't been ruled out, any blip in his recovery could cause a delay he can't come back from. He's also not as warmed up as he would be if he was returning in the regular season with a chance to go on a rehab assignment.
But Boston is desperate for a spark. If there's even a chance Mead could bring it, the Sox should let him try.

Mead was having a career year before his injury, and getting that version of him in the lineup could be huge for the Red Sox's offense. However, if he's not at 100%, it may not be the best idea for the Red Sox to stick him in the lineup at second base in the most important series of the year.
Mead was slashing .253/.353/.498 with 17 home runs before he went down. The Red Sox's options at second base in the postseason include Andruw Monasterio, Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Nick Sogard. However, if Willson Contreras is unable to play due to his hand injury, Sogard will likely draw the starts at first base.
If Contreras can't play, Mead's presence in the lineup may become more important. The Red Sox's offense has been scuffling lately, and Mead could provide a boost in October.
